title: Integrating local habitat structure and landscape heterogeneity is essential to conserve multitaxonomic biodiversity in European primary forests
content:
Our results demonstrate that the drivers of primary forest biodiversity are largely context-dependent; therefore, conservation strategies based on single biodiversity indicators or individual structural targets are likely to be ineffective. To mitigate the impacts of habitat loss and conserve the full spectrum of primary forest biodiversity, management should integrate a full range of local habitat structures within broader landscape-scale planning. Ensuring connectivity among remaining primary forest fragments will further facilitate dispersal across wider, human-modified landscapes. Coordinating local-level habitat retention with landscape-scale connectivity is therefore essential to safeguard these irreplaceable refugia and their biodiversity.


Abstract

Primary forests are important refugia for many species of conservation concern. In Europe, centuries of land-use change have severely restricted the extent of such forests to small, isolated fragments embedded within human-modified landscapes. However, despite the key role of European temperate primary forests in achieving regional conservation targets, it is still unclear how local habitat conditions and landscape-scale heterogeneity combine to shape primary forest communities. We examined how multiple biodiversity components respond to local structural versus landscape heterogeneity, exploring community drivers across the two most prevalent European temperate primary forest types—mixed-beech and monodominant spruce. To provide an evidence base for practitioners, we determined how wood-inhabiting fungi, saproxylic beetles, epiphytic and epixylic lichens, and birds, and their red-listed components, relate to habitat indicators from remote sensing, forest inventory data and detailed forest age data. In total, we identified 1229 species, including 254 classified as red-listed. Drivers of different community components were diverse and context-specific, varying between forest types and taxonomic groups. Overall, lichen, avian and fungal communities were primarily associated with local habitat structures indicative of long ecological continuity (e.g. old trees, deadwood), whereas beetle richness responded more strongly to landscape heterogeneity, but only in spruce forests. Across all taxa and forest types, patterns for red-listed species and community composition frequently diverged from those of all species, underscoring how single biodiversity metrics may fail to capture key impacts on species of conservation concern. Synthesis and applications. Our results demonstrate that the drivers of primary forest biodiversity are largely context-dependent; therefore, conservation strategies based on single biodiversity indicators or individual structural targets are likely to be ineffective. To mitigate the impacts of habitat loss and conserve the full spectrum of primary forest biodiversity, management should integrate a full range of local habitat structures within broader landscape-scale planning. Ensuring connectivity among remaining primary forest fragments will further facilitate dispersal across wider, human-modified landscapes. Coordinating local-level habitat retention with landscape-scale connectivity is therefore essential to safeguard these irreplaceable refugia and their biodiversity.
